title: The Year of Endings
teaser: Van Gogh dies in a wheatfield. William James maps the stream of consciousness. Emily Dickinson's secret poems emerge from a locked chest. At Wounded Knee, the Ghost Dance ends in massacre. The nineteenth century confronts its final frontiers — geographic, psychological, artistic.

image.caption: Vincent van Gogh, Wheatfield with Crows, July 1890. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam

art: In Auvers-sur-Oise, Vincent van Gogh paints seventy canvases in seventy days — a final eruption of creative intensity. Wheatfield with Crows, painted in July, shows a turbulent sky above golden wheat, three paths leading nowhere, black birds that might be arriving or departing. On July 27th, he shoots himself in a field; two days later, with his brother Theo at his side, he dies at thirty-seven. The Post-Impressionist revolution loses its most volatile champion, though almost no one knows it yet — Van Gogh sold only one or two paintings in his lifetime. In Paris, Claude Monet begins buying the land at Giverny where he will create his water garden; Paul Cézanne continues his solitary experiments in Aix. But the year's most consequential exhibition opens in Brussels: Les XX shows Van Gogh's work alongside Cézanne, Renoir, and Sisley — the first time these painters are exhibited as a coherent movement, shaping how the twentieth century will understand the birth of modern art.
lit: On November 12th, Poems by Emily Dickinson appears in print — 115 poems selected from the 1,800 her sister Lavinia discovered in a locked chest after the poet's death in 1886. Edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd, the collection is heavily altered to fit Victorian conventions: Dickinson's dashes become commas, her slant rhymes are 'corrected.' But even in bowdlerized form, the poems electrify readers. The book goes through eleven printings in two years. A secret life of radical poetry — written in isolation, shared with almost no one — emerges posthumously to reshape American literature. Meanwhile, in the July issue of Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, Oscar Wilde publishes The Picture of Dorian Gray: a portrait that ages while its subject stays young, a Faustian bargain about art, beauty, and moral corruption. Critics call it 'poisonous,' 'unclean.' Wilde revises and expands it into the 1891 novel. In Norway, Knut Hamsun publishes Hunger — the first stream-of-consciousness novel, tracing the irrational thoughts of a starving writer in Christiania. What James describes scientifically, Hamsun embodies literarily: consciousness as flow, not structure.
phil: William James publishes The Principles of Psychology — twelve years in the writing, 1,400 pages, and immediately recognized as a masterwork. James introduces the term 'stream of consciousness': thought is not a chain of discrete ideas but a continuous flow, 'a river' in which no two moments are identical. The self is not a substance but a process. He rejects both the associationist psychology that treats mind as passive and the physiological reductionism that treats it as merely brain. The implications ripple outward: if consciousness flows rather than steps, then perhaps narrative should too — a connection modernist novelists will soon exploit. Meanwhile, James George Frazer publishes the first edition of The Golden Bough (two volumes; it will grow to twelve), arguing that magic, religion, and science form a developmental sequence — that Christianity evolved from fertility cults, that the Crucifixion echoes dying-god myths from Osiris to Adonis. The Victorian synthesis cracks: religion becomes anthropology, myth becomes comparative literature.
hist: On December 29th, the 7th Cavalry surrounds a band of Miniconjou Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota. They have come to suppress the Ghost Dance, a millenarian movement promising that proper practice will reunite the living with ancestral spirits and end American expansion. When soldiers attempt to disarm the Lakota, a shot is fired — by whom remains disputed. The cavalry opens fire with Hotchkiss guns. Between 250 and 300 Lakota die, most of them unarmed women, children, and elders. Twenty soldiers receive the Medal of Honor. The massacre ends organized Native American resistance to westward expansion. The same year, the U.S. Census Bureau announces that a continuous frontier line no longer exists — the West is 'settled.' Three years later, Frederick Jackson Turner will argue that the closing of the frontier closes a chapter of American identity. In Europe, Bismarck is dismissed by Kaiser Wilhelm II; the steady hand that unified Germany yields to the volatile ambitions that will fragment it.
conn: The year's recurring motif is the end of the line — geographic, psychological, artistic. The frontier closes; Van Gogh's paths lead nowhere; the Ghost Dance's promise of renewal ends in massacre. William James shows that consciousness has no edges, only flow — and Hamsun immediately translates this into literary technique, proving that philosophy can generate form. Frazer's comparative method connects Christian redemption to pagan myth the same year Dickinson's private religion emerges from hiding: different strategies for the same crisis of meaning. Van Gogh painted the sky not as it looked but as it felt, which is exactly what James argued perception does — we don't receive the world passively but construct it from the stream. The fin de siècle anxiety is visible everywhere: what happens when old certainties dissolve and new ones haven't yet cohered? At Wounded Knee, one answer: violence. In Auvers, another: vision pushed to its limit, then silence.
funFact: Van Gogh's letters show he titled the painting Wheatfield with Crows matter-of-factly — the romantic reading of it as a 'suicide note' is entirely posthumous. He painted at least two more canvases after it.
